body.translated_text: <s>Tattvamīmāṃsā</s> (An Inquiry into the Nature of Reality)

body.text:
sukhaikaviṣayā bhūtānāṃ pravṛttiḥ / sukhaṃ ca sati duḥkhahetāvasambhavati / ato bhavati duḥkhābhighātake jijñāsā sā ca tattvajñānāt / atastattvamatra nirūpyate / nanu trividhaṃ duḥkham ādhyātmikamādhidaivikamādhibhautikaṃ ca / tatrādhyātmikaṃ dvividhaṃ śārīraṃ mānasañca / śārīraṃ vātapittaśleṣmaṇāṃ vaiṣamyanimittaṃ mānasaṃ kāmakrodhādinibandhanam / ādhibhautikaṃ mānuṣapaśupakṣyādinimittam / ādhidaivikaṃ yakṣarākṣasagrahādyāveśanibandhanam / teṣāṃ caiṣāṃ laukikairevopāyaiḥ pratīkāraḥ śakyate / tathā hi śārīrasyauṣadhādibhiḥ mānasasya manojñastrīpānabhojanavastrālaṅkārādiprāptyā ādhibhautikasya nītiśāstrābhyāsasusthānopaveśādinā ādhidaivikasya maṇimantrādyupayogeneti sukara upāyaḥ tattvajñānaṃ tvanekajanmaraparābhyāsasādhyam / tathā ca laukikānāmābhāṇakaḥ /
  akke cenmadhu vindeta kimarthaṃ parvataṃ vrajet /
  iṣṭasyārthasya saṃprāptau ko vidvān yatnamācaret // iti /
  akke gṛhakoṇe / maivam / na hyetairupāyaiḥ sarvameva duḥkhaṃ nivartate / nivṛttaṃ punarnotpadyate / yadyapi śāstrīyamapi ahorātramāsavarṣādisādhyamupāyāntaraṃ sukaraṃ śrūyate apāma somamamṛtā abhūmeti tathāpi etadapi laukikopāyatulyameva / tathāhi somayāgaḥ paśuvadhādisādhanatvānna viśeṣataḥ śuddhaḥ / akṛte hi tadvadhaprāyaścitte svargādigatyanantaraṃ paripacyate eva tadduḥkham / na ca na hiṃsyātsarvābhūtānīti sāmānyaśāstrabhya viśeṣaśāstreṇāgnīṣomīyaṃ paśumālabhetetyanena bādhaḥ śaṅkyaḥ bhinnaviṣayatvena bādhyabādhakabhāvāsambhavāt agnīṣomīyaṃ paśumālabheteti vākyena hi vadhasya kratūpakārakatvameva bodhyate na tu puruṣapratyavāyābhāvaḥ / evaṃ svargāderanityatvamapi sattve sati kāryatvādanumīyate / tathā ca śrutirapi
body.translated_text:
The activity of all beings is directed toward happiness alone. And happiness is impossible when the cause of suffering exists. Therefore, there arises a desire to know what destroys suffering, and that (knowledge) comes from the knowledge of <s>tattva</s> (reality/truth). Hence, <s>tattva</s> (reality) is here investigated. Now, suffering is threefold: <s>ādhyātmika</s> (pertaining to the self), <s>ādhidaivika</s> (pertaining to divine forces), and <s>ādhibhautika</s> (pertaining to external beings). Of these, <s>ādhyātmika</s> is of two kinds: bodily and mental. Bodily suffering is caused by the imbalance of <s>vāta</s> (wind), <s>pitta</s> (bile), and <s>śleṣman</s> (phlegm). Mental suffering is rooted in desire, anger, and similar (afflictions). <s>Ādhibhautika</s> (suffering from external beings) is caused by humans, animals, birds, and similar creatures. <s>Ādhidaivika</s> (suffering from divine forces) is rooted in possession by <s>Yakṣas</s>, <s>Rākṣasas</s>, <s>Grahas</s> (malign spirits), and others. And for all of these, remedies are possible through worldly means alone. For instance: for bodily suffering, through medicines and such; for mental suffering, through obtaining beautiful women, drink, food, garments, ornaments, and the like; for <s>ādhibhautika</s> suffering, through study of <s>nītiśāstra</s> (political science), choosing a safe dwelling, and similar measures; for <s>ādhidaivika</s> suffering, through the use of gems, <s>mantras</s>, and such — thus the remedy is easy. But the knowledge of <s>tattva</s> (reality) is achievable only through practice across many lifetimes. And thus goes the common saying:
"If one can find honey in the corner of one's house, why would one go to the mountain? When the desired object can be obtained (easily), what wise person would make an effort?" — thus.
<s>Akka</s> means 'in the corner of the house.' Not so! For these (worldly) means do not eliminate all suffering whatsoever. And once eliminated, (the suffering) does not arise again. Even though scriptural means — attainable through days, nights, months, and years — are heard of as easy alternatives, such as (the Vedic declaration) "We have drunk the <s>Soma</s>, we have become immortal," even so, this too is equal to worldly means. For the <s>Soma</s> sacrifice, being accomplished through the killing of animals and such, is not specifically pure. For when the <s>prāyaścitta</s> (expiation) for that killing is not performed, the suffering from it will surely ripen after the attainment of heaven and other destinations. Nor should one suspect that the general scripture "One should not harm any living beings" is overridden by the specific scripture "One should sacrifice the <s>Agnīṣomīya</s> (fire-and-Soma) animal," since there is no relation of the overriding and overridden because they have different domains. For the statement "One should sacrifice the <s>Agnīṣomīya</s> animal" conveys only that the killing is instrumental to the sacrifice, not that the person incurs no fault. Thus, even the impermanence of heaven and other (realms) is inferred because, being an effect, (they must be) impermanent. And the <s>śruti</s> (Vedic revelation) also (says):

children.text: na karmaṇā na prajayā dhanena tyāgenaikenāmṛtatvamānaśuḥ /
children.translated_text: "Not through ritual action, nor through progeny, nor through wealth — through renunciation alone have they attained immortality."

children.text: pareṇa nākaṃ nihitaṃ guhāyāṃ vibhrājate yadyatayo viśanti //
children.translated_text: "That which is beyond heaven, hidden in the cave (of the heart), shines forth — which the ascetics enter."

body.text: karmaṇā jyotiṣṭomādinā prajayā putreṇa dhanena devatājñānena putreṇāyaṃ loko jeyo vidyayā devalokaḥ karmaṇā pitṛloka iti śrutyantarāt ebhiḥ pitrādilokasyaiva prāptirnāmṛtatvasyeti bhāvaha / tarhi kathamamṛtatvamityata āha tyāgeneti / sarvakarmasaṃnyāsasādhyajñānenetyarthaḥ / tadamṛtatvaṃ svarga eva cettattrāha pareṇa nākamiti / tarhi dūrasthatvānna prāpyamiti cettatrāha nihitaṃ guhāyāmiti / taccāsannatvātpṛthak janairapi labhyamiti cettatrāha yadyataya iti / adūrabhūtamapyavivekināṃ dūrabhūtameva / tathā śrutyantaram /
body.translated_text: By <s>karman</s> (ritual action) is meant the <s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s> and other (sacrifices). By <s>prajā</s> (progeny) is meant a son. By <s>dhana</s> (wealth) is meant knowledge of the deity — as another <s>śruti</s> says: "By a son, this world is won; by knowledge, the world of the gods; by ritual action, the world of the fathers." Through these, only the attainment of the worlds of the fathers and others (is possible), not of immortality — such is the purport. Then how is immortality (attained)? To this he says: "Through renunciation" — meaning through knowledge attainable by the renunciation of all ritual actions. If that immortality is heaven itself, then (the text) says: "Beyond heaven." If (one objects that) it cannot be attained because it is far away, then (the text) says: "Hidden in the cave (of the heart)." And if (one says that) because it is near, it can be obtained by ordinary people too, then (the text) says: "Which the ascetics (enter)" — even what is not far, for those without discrimination, is indeed far. And another <s>śruti</s> (says):

children.translated_text: "Through ritual action, the sages who desired progeny and wealth warded off death."

children.text: tathā 'pare ṛṣayo ye manīṣiṇaḥ paraṃ karmabhyo 'mṛtatvamānaśuriti //
children.translated_text: "And other sages, those wise ones, attained immortality beyond (ritual) actions."

body.text:
apāma somamamṛtā abhūmetyamṛtatvābhidhānaṃ tu cirasthityabhiprāyam / yadāhuḥ ābhūtasamplavaṃ sthānamamṛtatvaṃ hi bhāṣyate iti / tadetatsarvamabhipretyoktaṃ śāstrakṛdbhiḥ tadbiparītaḥ śreyān vyaktāvyaktajñavijñānāt / asyārthaḥ / tasmātsomapānāderaviśuddhādanityāt viparīto hiṃsādyasaṅkarādviśuddha upāyaḥ śreyān / sa ca katham ? vyaktasya kāryajātasya tatkāraṇasya avyaktasya pradhānasya tābhyāṃ parasya tasyātmanaśca vivekena jñānādbhavati iti / na ca vivekotpannaphalasyāpi kāryatvādanityatvaṃ śaṃkyam / bhāvarūpakāryasyaivānityatvāt duḥkhadhvaṃsasya tu kāryatve 'pi nityatvāt /
  athātra śāstre catasro vidhāḥ / prakṛtirvikṛtirubhayamanubhayañceti / tatra jagato mūlakāraṇabhūtaṃ pradhānaṃ na vikāraḥ kintu prakṛtireva prakarotīti prakṛtiḥ sattvarajastamasāṃ sāmyāvasthā / asyāśca mūlāntaramanavasthābhayānnāstīti mūlaprakṛtirityucyate / saiva śāstrāntare avidyā māyāśabdenocyate / etadevāvyaktaṃ sattvādīnāṃ guṇānāṃ vaiṣamye sati vyaktamityucyate / yathāhi samudrajale calitācalitapradeśāḥ / evaṃ triguṇātmike pradhāne pariṇāmavāṃstadvidhuraśca pradeśaḥ / tatra prakṛtivikāreṣu madhye ādyo vikāro mahānityucyate sa etadbuddhilakṣaṇaḥ / sa āha mahānsāttviko rājasastāmasaśceti trividhaḥ / buddhestu prathamo vikāro 'haṅkāraḥ / ete ca mahadādayaḥ prakṛtayo vikṛtayaśca / tathāhi mahattattvamahaṅkārasya prakṛtirvikṛtiśca mūlaprakṛteḥ / ayaṃ hi kramaḥ prakṛtermahān mahato 'haṅkāraṃ ahaṅkārātpañca tanmātrāḥ tābhyaḥ pañca bhūtāni tanmātrāṇi punaḥ kṣīradadhyorantarāle kalalapariṇāmātpariṇatāni sūkṣmabhūtāni kusumasaurabhyena sūkṣmasthūlatayopalakṣyamāṇaṃ guṇavaiṣamyameva tanmātraśabdena bhūtaśabdena cocyate / pañca bhūtāni ekādaśendriyāṇi ceti eṣa ṣoḍaśako gaṇastu vikāra eva na prakṛtiḥ / puruṣastvātmā na prakṛtirna vikṛtiḥ / tadetadāhuḥ /
body.translated_text: The [Vedic verse] 'We have drunk <s>Soma</s>, we have become immortal' (<s>apāma somamamṛtā abhūma</s>) — the designation of immortality here is intended in the sense of enduring for a long time. As [the commentators] say: 'Enduring as long as the existence of the world is called immortality.' All of this, keeping [these points] in mind, was stated by the authors of the [philosophical] treatises [in the verse]: 'The opposite [of the soma-drinking path] is better, because of the knowledge that discriminates the manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower.' Its meaning is: therefore, the means that is opposite [to drinking soma] and the like — which is impure and impermanent — is better: [the means] that is pure, free from mixture with violence and the like. And how does that [come about]? It comes about through the knowledge by discrimination (<s>viveka</s>) of the manifest (<s>vyakta</s>) — the class of effects — of the unmanifest (<s>avyakta</s>), which is the primary matter (<s>pradhāna</s>) and the cause of those [effects] — and of the <s>ātman</s> (self) which is other than and beyond both of those. And there need be no apprehension that, because [the fruit arising from discrimination] is itself a product, it is therefore impermanent; for only a product that is a positive entity is impermanent, whereas the destruction of suffering (<s>duḥkhadhvaṃsa</s>), even though it is a product, is permanent [i.e., the liberation once attained does not lapse]. Now in this [Sāṃkhya] treatise there are four [ontological] classes: <s>prakṛti</s> (primary nature), <s>vikṛti</s> (modification), both [<s>prakṛti</s> and <s>vikṛti</s>], and neither. Among these, <s>pradhāna</s> (the primary [matter]), which is the root cause of the universe, is not a modification (<s>vikāra</s>) but only a <s>prakṛti</s> (producer), since it produces — thus [it is called] <s>prakṛti</s>: the state of equilibrium of <s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s>. And because there is no other root [prior to it] — for fear of an infinite regress — it is called the <s>mūlaprakṛti</s> (root-nature). This same [entity] is called by the terms <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) and <s>māyā</s> in other treatises. This same [root-nature] is the <s>avyakta</s> (unmanifest); when there is inequality among the qualities (<s>guṇas</s>) such as <s>sattva</s> etc., it is called the <s>vyakta</s> (manifest) — just as in ocean water there are regions [that are] agitated and [regions that are] unagitated. Thus, in the <s>pradhāna</s> consisting of the three qualities (<s>triguṇātmaka</s>), there is [a region that] undergoes transformation and [a region] free from transformation. Among the modifications of <s>prakṛti</s>, the first modification is called <s>mahat</s> (the great [principle]); it has the characteristic of <s>buddhi</s> (intellect). That [<s>mahat</s>] is said to be threefold: <s>sāttvika</s>, <s>rājasa</s>, and <s>tāmasa</s>. And the first modification of <s>buddhi</s> is <s>ahaṃkāra</s> (ego-sense). These — [beginning with] <s>mahat</s> and so forth — are both <s>prakṛtis</s> and <s>vikṛtis</s>. For <s>mahattattva</s> is both a <s>prakṛti</s> (producer) of <s>ahaṃkāra</s> and a <s>vikṛti</s> (modification) of the root-<s>prakṛti</s>. The sequence is: from <s>prakṛti</s> [comes] <s>mahat</s>; from <s>mahat</s>, <s>ahaṃkāra</s>; from <s>ahaṃkāra</s>, the five <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements); from these, the five gross elements (<s>bhūtas</s>). The <s>tanmātras</s>, however, are subtle elements transformed at the intermediate stage between milk and curds — the subtle-to-coarse distinction indicated by, e.g., the fragrance of a flower — and this unevenness of qualities alone is called by the term '<s>tanmātra</s>' and also by the term '<s>bhūta</s>.' The five gross elements (<s>bhūtas</s>) and the eleven sense organs (<s>indriyas</s>): this group of sixteen is only a modification (<s>vikāra</s>) and not a <s>prakṛti</s>. And the <s>puruṣa</s> (spirit/self) is <s>ātman</s> — neither <s>prakṛti</s> nor <s>vikṛti</s>. Thus this has been stated [in verse]:

body.text:
mūlaprakṛtiravikṛtirmahadādyāḥ prakṛtivikṛtayaḥ sapta /
ṣoḍaśakastu vikāro na prakṛtirna vikṛtiḥ puruṣaḥ // iti /
body.translated_text:
The root-<s>prakṛti</s> (<s>mūlaprakṛti</s>) is non-modified (<s>avikṛti</s>); the seven — [beginning with] <s>mahat</s> etc. — are both <s>prakṛti</s> and modification (<s>vikṛti</s>);
the group of sixteen is only modification; <s>puruṣa</s> is neither <s>prakṛti</s> nor modification.

body.text:
atha śāstraparibhāṣā / dṛṣṭamanumānamāptavacanañceti trividhaṃ laukikaṃ pramāṇam / ārṣaṃ tu vijñānaṃ yogināmeveti tadatra noktam / tatra pṛthivyādayaḥ sukhādayaścāsmadādīnāṃ viṣayāḥ / tanmātralakṣaṇāstu devānāṃ yogināṃ ca viṣayā na tvasmadādīnām teṣāṃ cendriyaiḥ sambandhaḥ sannikarṣaḥ / evañca viṣayasambaddhendriyāśrito yo buddhidharmo 'dhyavasāyaḥ sa eva pramāṇam / ayaṃ hi kramaḥ / viṣayasambaddhānāmindriyāṇāṃ vṛttau satyāṃ buddhestu tamobhibhave sati yaḥ sattvasamudrekaḥ so 'dhyavasāya iti jñānamiti vṛttiścākhyāyate / tadidaṃ pratyakṣapramāṇam / asmācca yaścetanāśakteranugrahastatphalaṃ pramā bodhaḥ / buddhisattvaṃ hi prākṛtatvādacetanamiti tadīyo 'dhyavasāyo 'pyacetanaḥ ghaṭādivat / evaṃ hi buddhisattvasya pariṇāmabhedāḥ sukhādayo 'pyacetanāḥ / puruṣastu sukhādyananuṣaṅgī cetanaḥ / so 'yaṃ buddhitattvavarttinā jñānasukhādinā tatpratibimbito buddhisādṛśyaprāptyā jñānasukhādimāniva bhavati citisādṛśyaprāptyā ca acetanāpi buddhistadavadhyavasāyaśca cetana iva bhavati / cārvākāstu pratyakṣānyat na mānamiti vadanti / tanmate saṃdigdhaviparyayastu puruṣabodhanaṃ nopapadyeta / nahi puruṣāntaragataḥ saṃśayaḥ anumānaṃ kathanaṃ vinā vā jñātuṃ śakyaḥ /
  pramāṇāntarāṇi tvatraivāntarbhavanti / tathāhi upamānaṃ tāvat gosadṛśo gavaya iti vākyaṃ tajjanito bodho śabda evāntarbhavati cakṣuḥsaṃnikṛṣṭasya gavayasya yat gosādṛśyajñānaṃ tatpratyakṣameva / evaṃ jīvataścaitrasya gṛhāsattvena bahiḥsattvakalpanamarthāpattiḥ sāpyanumāna evāntarbhavati / vimataścaitro bahirbhavitumarhati gṛheṣvavidyamānatvāt / yadā tvavyāpakaḥ sannekatrāsti tadānyatra nāsti yadaikatra nāsti tadānyatrāstīti vyāptigrahāt / evamiha vaṭe yakṣaḥ prativasati iti aitihyaṃ na pramāṇamanirdiṣṭasvavaktṛkatvena sandehāt / āptoktatvaniścaye tvāgama eva / evamabhāvo nānupalabdhigamyaḥ kintu pratyakṣa eva / na hi bhūtalasya kaivalyalakṣaṇātpariṇāmaviśeṣādanyo ghaṭābhāvo nāma / sarva eva hi bhāvāḥ pratikṣaṇaṃ pariṇāminaḥ sa ca pariṇāmabheda aindriyaka evetyalam /
  tatra sūkṣmasyāvyaktasyāpratyakṣatve 'pi mahadādikāryeṇa tadanumīyate / tathāhi sadeva kāryaṃ kāraṇavyāpārātprāgapi / asato hi sattvaṃ duṣkaram nahi nīlaṃ śilpisahasreṇāpi pītaṃ śakyaṃ kartum / kintu tileṣu pīḍanena tailasyeva āvirbhāvamātramutpattiḥ tirobhāva eva vināśaḥ / kiñcāsambaddhasyāpi kāryasya janyatve sambaddhatvāviśeṣātsarvaṃ kāryaṃ sarvasmādbhavediti kāryasambaddhasyaiva kāraṇasya janakatvamupeyam / na ca sadasatoḥ sambandho 'stīti satkāryam / kiñca tantudharmatvāttantūpādeyatvācca na paṭasyārthāntaratvam yannaivaṃ tannaivaṃ yathā ghaṭapaṭau / tathā arthāntarayoḥ saṃyogo vā bhavati yathā kuṃḍabadarayoḥ aprāptirvā bhavati himavadvindhyayoḥ / tasmādyathā kūrmaśarīre kūrmāṅgāni niviśamānāni tirobhavanti na tatra tānyutpadyante na vinaśyanti vā evamekasmātsuvarṇādermukuṭādiprādurbhāva evotpattiḥ / evañca mahadādikāryaṃ pradhāne 'bhiniviśate avyaktaṃ bhavati iti / kāraṇe sattyeva kāryasya vibhāgāvibhāgābhyāmavyaktaṃ kāraṇamastīti gamyate / taccāvyaktaṃ nityaṃ vyāpakaṃ ca sarvaṃ kāryaṃ vyāpnoti tathā niḥkriyaṃ kvacidapyanāśritañca evaṃ niravayavaṃ svatantraṃ ca / etadviparītantu vyaktam / evaṃ vyaktamavyaktaṃ ca sukhaduḥkhamoharūpaguṇatrayānvitamacetanaṃ prasavadharmi ca tadviparītaḥ puruṣaḥ sukhādayaśca guṇāḥ sattvarajastamorūpāḥ / sattvasya prayojanaṃ tu prakāśaḥ rajastu tasya pravartakaṃ tamastu niyāmakaṃ yadi hi tamasā guruṇā niyamyeta tadā rajaḥ laghu sattvaṃ sarvatra pravarttayet / yathā sattvaṃ rajastamasī abhibhūya śāntā vṛttimadhigacchati yathā ca rajaḥ sattvarajasī abhibhūya ghorāṃ tathā tamaḥ sattvarajasī abhibhūya mūḍhāmiti / yadyapyete parasparaṃ virodhaśīlāḥ tathāpi yathā vātapittaśleṣmāṇaḥ parasparavirodhinaḥ śarīradhāraṇarūpaikakāryakāriṇaḥ evamete 'pi / evaṃ sukhahetutvātsattvaṃ sukhātmakaṃ duḥkhahetutvādduḥkhātmakaṃ rajaḥ yanmohakaṃ tattamaḥ / te ca sukhaduḥkhamohāḥ parasparavirodhinaḥ svānurūpāṇyeva parasparaṃ viruddhāni sukhaduḥkhamohātmakāni nimittāni kalpayanti / tathāhi ekaiva strī svāminaṃ prati sukharūpasadbhāvāttaṃ sukhākaroti sapatnīstu duḥkhākaroti evamatrāpyekasyāpi nimittabhedādbhedaḥ / sukhaprakāśalāghavaistu parasparamavirodhānna nimittabhedāḥ kalpyante / sargādau tu pariṇāmasvabhāvā guṇāḥ kṣaṇamapyapariṇamayya na tiṣṭhantīti sattvaṃ sattvarūpatayā rajo rajorūpatayā tamastamorūpatayā pravarttate / yathāhi ghanavimuktajalānāṃ jambīrakaravīranārikerādyāśrayabhedādasti bhedaḥ evamekarūpāṇāmapi guṇānāṃ pratiguṇāśrayaviśeṣādanekarūpatā / ātmā tu vyaktāvyaktasaṃghātabhinnaḥ / parārtho hi saṃghāto bhavati / yathā śayanāsanādayaḥ saṃghātāḥ śarīrārthā dṛṣṭāḥ / kiñca yathā rathādi yaṃtryādinādhiṣṭhitaṃ evaṃ triguṇātmakamapi pareṇa kenacidadhiṣṭhīyamānaṃ yuktam / sa cātmā pratiśarīraṃ bhinnaḥ na hyekasmin sukhini sarve sukhinaḥ / sa cāyaṃ puruṣaḥ sākṣī ca bhavati prakṛtirhi svaviṣayacaritaṃ puruṣāya pradarśayati / tathāhi loke arthipratyarthinau vivādaviṣayaṃ sākṣiṇe darśayataḥ / evaṃ cāyaṃ draṣṭāpi bhavati / tathā atraiguṇādasya kaivalyaṃ ca dharmaḥ / ātyantiko hi duḥkhatrayābhāvaḥ kaivalyam / ata evātriguṇatvānmadhyastho 'pi bhavati sukhī hi sukhe tṛpyan duḥkhī dviṣan madhyastho na bhavati / āta evobhayarāhityādudāsīna ityucyate / evamaprasavadharmitādakartā 'pi / yadyapi cetano 'haṃ karomīti kṛticaitanyayoraikādhikaraṇyaṃ pratīyate tathāpi puruṣapradhānādisambandhātpuruṣacaitanyamavyakte guṇakartṛtvaṃ ca puruṣe upacaryate / bhogyaṃ hi pradhānaṃ bhoktāramantareṇa na saṃbhavati iti bhavati tasya bhoktrapekṣā puruṣastu bhogyena pradhānena saṃyuktastadgataṃ duḥkhamātmanyabhimanyamānaḥ kaivalyaṃ prārthayate / tacca sattvapuruṣānyatākhyātinibandhanam na ca sattvapuruṣānyatākhyātiḥ pradhānamantareṇeti kaivalyārthaṃ puruṣaḥ pradhānamapekṣata iti tayoḥ saṃyogaḥ ata eva saṃyogo na mahadādisargamantareṇa bhogāya kaivalyāya ca paryāpta iti saṃyoga eva bhogāpavargārthaṃ sargaṃ karotīti //

Now, the technical terminology of the system. There are three kinds of worldly <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge): <s>dṛṣṭa</s> (perception), <s>anumāna</s> (inference), and <s>āptavacana</s> (testimony of the trustworthy). But the knowledge of sages (<s>ārṣa vijñāna</s>) belongs to <s>yogins</s> alone, and so it is not discussed here. Among these, earth and other (elements), and pleasure and other (qualities) are the objects of perception for beings like us. But <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements) are objects for gods and <s>yogins</s>, not for us. And the connection of those (objects) with the senses is <s>sannikarṣa</s> (contact). Thus, the quality of <s>buddhi</s> (intellect) that depends on sense-organs connected with their objects — namely, <s>adhyavasāya</s> (determinate cognition) — is itself the <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge). This is the sequence: when the sense-organs connected with objects are functioning, and when <s>tamas</s> (darkness/inertia) is overcome in <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), the predominance of <s>sattva</s> (luminosity) — that is called <s>adhyavasāya</s> (determination), or <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge), or <s>vṛtti</s> (mental operation). This is <s>pratyakṣa pramāṇa</s> (perceptual knowledge). And the grace of the sentient power (<s>cetanā śakti</s>) upon this — that result is <s>pramā</s> (true cognition), awareness. For the <s>sattva</s> (purity-component) of <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), being a product of <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature), is non-sentient; hence its <s>adhyavasāya</s> (determination) too is non-sentient, like a pot and such. Likewise, the modifications of the <s>sattva</s> of <s>buddhi</s> — pleasure and others — are also non-sentient. But <s>Puruṣa</s> (the Self) is sentient, unattached to pleasure and such. This <s>Puruṣa</s>, reflected in the knowledge and pleasure residing in <s>buddhi-tattva</s> (the principle of intellect), appears as if possessing knowledge and pleasure by acquiring the likeness of <s>buddhi</s>; and <s>buddhi</s>, though non-sentient, by acquiring the likeness of <s>citi</s> (consciousness), along with its determinations, appears as if sentient. The <s>Cārvākas</s> (materialists), however, say that there is no valid means of knowledge other than perception. In their view, informing a person about doubt and error would be impossible, for the doubt residing in another person cannot be known without inference and verbal communication.
Other <s>pramāṇas</s> are subsumed within these very ones. For instance, <s>upamāna</s> (comparison) — the sentence "A <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox) is similar to a cow" and the cognition arising from it are subsumed under <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony); while the cognition of the <s>gavaya</s>'s similarity to a cow when the <s>gavaya</s> is in contact with the eye is nothing but <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception). Similarly, <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) — such as presuming that the living <s>Caitra</s>, not being in the house, must be outside — is subsumed under <s>anumāna</s> (inference): "The missing <s>Caitra</s> must be outside, because he is not found in the house." When something that is not pervasive exists in one place, then it does not exist elsewhere; and when it does not exist in one place, then it exists elsewhere — this is the grasping of <s>vyāpti</s> (invariable concomitance). Likewise, <s>aitihya</s> (tradition), such as "A <s>Yakṣa</s> dwells in this banyan tree," is not a valid means of knowledge, because its original speaker is unidentified, leading to doubt. But when it is certain that a trustworthy person said it, then it is simply <s>āgama</s> (scriptural testimony). Similarly, absence (<s>abhāva</s>) is not known through <s>anupalabdhi</s> (non-apprehension) but through <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) itself. For the absence of a pot is nothing other than the bare ground's particular state of transformation, characterized by its being unaccompanied (by the pot). For all entities are constantly undergoing transformation, and that transformation is itself perceptible — enough said.
Regarding the subtle and unmanifest — even though it is imperceptible — it is inferred through its effects such as <s>Mahat</s> (the Great Principle) and others. For the effect exists even before the operation of the cause. The production of a non-existent thing is impossible — for even a thousand craftsmen cannot make blue into yellow. Rather, production is merely the manifestation (of what already exists), like oil from sesame seeds through pressing, and destruction is merely the disappearance (of the manifest form). Moreover, if even an unrelated effect could be produced, then by the absence of any distinctive (causal) relation, everything would be the effect of everything — therefore, it must be accepted that only the cause related to a specific effect has the power to produce it. And since there can be no relation between the existent and the non-existent, the effect must (pre-)exist in the cause (<s>satkāryavāda</s>). Furthermore, since cloth possesses the properties of the threads and since the threads are its material cause, cloth is not something entirely different (from the threads). What is not so is not so — as with a pot and a cloth (which are different from each other). Between truly different things, there is either conjunction, as between a bowl and jujubes, or non-contact, as between the <s>Himālaya</s> and <s>Vindhya</s> mountains. Therefore, just as the limbs of a tortoise, withdrawing into the tortoise's body, disappear but are not produced there nor destroyed, in the same way production is merely the emergence (of a crown, etc.) from the single (substance of) gold. And thus the effects such as <s>Mahat</s> (the Great Principle) merge back into <s>Pradhāna</s> (the Primal Cause) and become <s>avyakta</s> (unmanifest). Since the effect exists in the cause itself, through (the distinction of) differentiation and non-differentiation, it is understood that the unmanifest cause exists. And that <s>Avyakta</s> (Unmanifest) is eternal, all-pervading — pervading all effects — likewise inactive, not dependent on anything, without parts, and independent. The <s>Vyakta</s> (Manifest), however, is the opposite. Thus, both the <s>Vyakta</s> and <s>Avyakta</s> are endowed with the three <s>guṇas</s> (qualities) whose nature is pleasure, pain, and delusion; they are non-sentient and generative. The <s>Puruṣa</s> (Self) is the opposite. And the <s>guṇas</s> — pleasure and others — have the nature of <s>sattva</s> (luminosity), <s>rajas</s> (activity), and <s>tamas</s> (inertia). The function of <s>sattva</s> is illumination; <s>rajas</s> is the activator; <s>tamas</s> is the restrainer — for if <s>tamas</s>, being heavy, restrains, then <s>rajas</s>, being light, would set <s>sattva</s> in motion everywhere. Just as <s>sattva</s>, overcoming <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>, attains a calm state; and just as <s>rajas</s>, overcoming <s>sattva</s> and <s>tamas</s>, attains a terrible state; so <s>tamas</s>, overcoming <s>sattva</s> and <s>rajas</s>, attains a state of delusion. Although these are mutually antagonistic by nature, nevertheless, just as <s>vāta</s> (wind), <s>pitta</s> (bile), and <s>śleṣman</s> (phlegm), though mutually opposed, cooperate in a single function — sustaining the body — so too do these. Thus, because it causes pleasure, <s>sattva</s> is of the nature of pleasure; because it causes pain, <s>rajas</s> is of the nature of pain; and that which deludes is <s>tamas</s>. And these — pleasure, pain, and delusion — being mutually opposed, each produces only causes that are of its own kind, i.e., mutually opposed (pleasure-producing, pain-producing, delusion-producing). For instance, the same woman, being pleasurable in nature to her husband, makes him happy, but makes her co-wives unhappy — thus even in a single case, there is differentiation due to difference in the occasioning factors. But since pleasure, illumination, and lightness are not mutually contradictory, no differentiation of their occasioning factors is posited (for <s>sattva</s>). At the beginning of creation, the <s>guṇas</s>, whose nature is transformation, do not remain even for a moment without transforming — so <s>sattva</s> evolves as <s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s> as <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s> as <s>tamas</s>. Just as waters released from a cloud differ according to their receptacles — lemon, oleander, coconut, etc. — so too the <s>guṇas</s>, though uniform in themselves, take on manifold forms due to the particular receptacles of each <s>guṇa</s>. The <s>Ātman</s> (Self) is different from the aggregate of <s>Vyakta</s> (Manifest) and <s>Avyakta</s> (Unmanifest). For an aggregate exists for the sake of another. Just as aggregates like beds and seats are seen to serve the body. Moreover, just as a chariot is controlled by a charioteer, so too the three-<s>guṇa</s> aggregate is reasonably controlled by some other (entity). And that <s>Ātman</s> is different in each body — for when one person is happy, not all are happy. And this <s>Puruṣa</s> is a witness, for <s>Prakṛti</s> (nature) displays to <s>Puruṣa</s> the activities performed in its own domain. Just as in the world, a plaintiff and defendant display the subject of their dispute to a witness. Thus, this (<s>Puruṣa</s>) is also a seer. Likewise, freedom from the three <s>guṇas</s> and <s>kaivalya</s> (absolute isolation) are its characteristics. For <s>kaivalya</s> is the complete and final absence of the threefold suffering. And precisely because of being free from the three <s>guṇas</s>, (the <s>Puruṣa</s>) is also neutral — for one who is happy, being satisfied in pleasure, or one who is suffering, being averse, is not neutral. Precisely for this reason, being free from both, it is called <s>udāsīna</s> (indifferent). Likewise, because of being non-productive, it is also a non-doer. Although the thought "I, being conscious, am acting" appears, (suggesting) that action and consciousness share the same locus, nevertheless, due to the connection of <s>Puruṣa</s> with <s>Pradhāna</s> (the Primal Cause) and others, the consciousness of <s>Puruṣa</s> is figuratively attributed to the <s>Avyakta</s>, and the agency of the <s>guṇas</s> is figuratively attributed to <s>Puruṣa</s>. For <s>Pradhāna</s>, being the object of enjoyment, cannot exist without an enjoyer — hence its dependence on the enjoyer. And <s>Puruṣa</s>, conjoined with <s>Pradhāna</s> (the object of enjoyment), erroneously attributing the suffering belonging to <s>Pradhāna</s> to itself, desires <s>kaivalya</s> (liberation). And that (<s>kaivalya</s>) is founded upon the discrimination between <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s> (<s>sattvapuruṣānyatākhyāti</s>). And this discrimination between <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s> is not possible without <s>Pradhāna</s> — therefore, for the sake of <s>kaivalya</s>, <s>Puruṣa</s> requires <s>Pradhāna</s> — hence their conjunction. And precisely for this reason, the conjunction alone, not being sufficient for enjoyment and liberation without the creation of <s>Mahat</s> and other (evolutes), produces creation for the sake of enjoyment and liberation.

atha vivekajñānopayoginī buddhirnirūpyate / tasyāśca vyāpāro 'dhyavasāyaḥ tadabhinnaḥ / eṣa buddherlakṣaṇaṃ samānāsamānajātīyavyavacchedakatvāt / tathāhi sarvo 'pi vyavahartā 'hamatrādhikṛta iti abhimatya mayā etatkartavyamiti adhyavasyati tataśca pravartate / tatra citisannidhānādāpannacaitanyāyā buddheryo 'yaṃ kartavyamiti viniśayayaḥ so 'dhyavasāyaḥ / tatra dharmo yāgādyanuṣṭhānajanitaḥ / jñānaṃ guṇapuruṣānyatākhyātiḥ / vairāgyaṃ rāgābhāvaḥ / evamaiśvaryamapi buddhidharmo yato 'ṇimādiprādurbhāvaḥ / ahamatra śaktaḥ matto nānyo 'trādhikṛtaḥ ato 'hamasmi ityādiko yo 'bhimānaḥ so 'haṅkāravyāpāratvādahaṅkāraḥ / tamupajīvya hi buddhiradhyavasyati karttavyametanmayeti ahaṅkārācca dvividhaḥ sargaḥ sāttvikādekādaśendriyāṇi tāmasāttu pañcatanmātrāḥ / rajasastu tatpravartakatvamātrātkāraṇatvam / sāttvikarājasatāmasāhaṅkārāṇāmeva krameṇa vaikārikastaijaso bhūtādiriti saṃjñāḥ / cakṣuḥśrotraghrāṇarasanatvagākhyāni buddhīndriyāṇi / vākpāṇipādapāyūpasthāni karmendriyāṇi / mana ubhayātmakaṃ buddhīndriyaṃ karmendriyañca / cakṣurādīnāṃ ca manodhiṣṭhitānāṃ svaviṣayeṣu pravṛtteḥ / prathamaṃ vastudarśanantantaraṃ bālamūkādivannirvikalpātmakaṃ sāmānyato jñānamutpadyate / paścācca vastudhamairjātyādibhiryo 'dhyavasāyaḥ sa saṅkalpākhyo manaso vyāpāraḥ / ekasmādahaṅkārādekādaśavidhāni indriyāṇi bhavantītyatra tu śabdādyupabhogasampravartakādṛṣṭabheda eva niyāmakaḥ / adṛṣṭabhedastu guṇapariṇāma eva / pañcabuddhīndriyāṇāṃ sambaddhavastvālocanaṃ vṛttiḥ vāgādikarmendriyāṇāṃ tu vacanādayo vṛttayaḥ / evaṃ mahato 'dhyavasāyaḥ ahaṅkārasyābhimānaḥ saṅkalpo manaso vṛttirvyāpāraḥ / kāryakaraṇābhimukhānāṃ karaṇānāṃ vṛttisaṅkarastu na bhavati / yathāhi parāvaskandāya pravṛttāḥ śāktīkayāṣṭīkādayaḥ svaṃ svaṃ śaktyādikamevādadate na parasparayaṣṭyādikam / nanu yāṣṭīkānāṃ cetanatvādastu tathā pravṛttiḥ karaṇānāṃ tvacetanānāṃ pravṛtterayuktatvāttatsvarūpasāmarthyopabhogābhijña adhiṣṭhātā svīkārya iti cenna tatpravṛttau puruṣārthasya hetutvāt etaccopapādayiṣyati / karaṇāni tu trayodaśa / karaṇatvaṃ tu śabdasparśādiprakāśanaṃ karmendriyāṇāṃ tu vacanādivyāpāraḥ / etadbāhyakaraṇaṃ varttamānakālamantaṣkaraṇaṃ tu trikālam / nadīpūrabhedādabhūdvṛṣṭiḥ asti dhūmādihāgniḥ pipīlikāṇḍasaṃcaraṇādbhaviṣyati vṛṣṭiriti pratyayāt / ye tu vaiśeṣikāḥ kālamekamatiriktaṃ svīkurvate / tanmate 'pyatītānāgatādivyavahārabhedaḥ upādhibhedādeva bhavati evaṃ ca taistairupādhibhirevātītānāgatādibhedasiddhau kimatiriktakālasvīkāreṇeti sāṃkhyāḥ / eṣāṃ cendriyāṇāma pradhānāpradhānabhāvo 'pyasti / yathāhi grāmādhyakṣā karṣakādibhyaḥ karamādāya viṣayādhyakṣāya prayacchanti viṣayādhyakṣaśca sarvādhyakṣāya sa ca bhūpataye evaṃ bāhyendriyāṇyālocya manase samarpayanti manaśca saṅkalpyāhaṅkārāya ahaṅkāraścābhimatya buddhau sarvādhyakṣāyāmiti / ete ca buddhīndriyamanohaṅkārā guṇaviśeṣā guṇānāṃ sattvarajastamasāṃ vikārāḥ parasparaṃ viruddhāṃ api puruṣārthenaikavākyatāpannāḥ yathā santamasāpanayanena prakāśāya militā vartitailavahnayaḥ pradīpo bhavati / nanu kasmādbuddhau prayacchanti na punarahaṅkārāya manase veti cenna puruṣārthasya prayojakatayā sākṣātsādhanaṃ pradhānaṃ buddhireva ahaṅkārādayastu taṃ prati gauṇāḥ / asmadādibhiḥ parasparavyāvṛttāni nānubhūyante iti śabdāditanmātrāṇi aviśeṣāḥ sūkṣmāṇi ca / ākāśādiṣu tu sthūleṣu kvacitsattvapradhānatayā śāntāḥ sukhāḥ prasannā laghavaḥ kecidrajastamaḥpradhānatayā ghorā mūḍhāśca / te viśeṣāḥ punaḥ tridhā sūkṣmaṃ śarīraṃ mātāpitṛjaṃ mahābhūtāni ca / pradhānenādisarge pratipuruṣamekaikamutpāditaṃ tathā 'vyāhataṃ śilāmapyanupraviśati / sargādāmahāpralayamavatiṣṭhate sūkṣmaṃ śarīraṃ tacca mahadahaṅkāraikādaśendriyapañcatanmātrasamudāyaḥ / etacca śarīraṃ bhogānarha iti sthūlaṃ śarīraṃ ṣāṭkauśikamāśrayati / lomalohitamāṃsāni mātṛtaḥ snāyvasthimajjānaḥ pitṛta iti ṣaṭ kośāḥ / nanu dharmādharmanimittaḥ saṃsāraḥ tasya ca sūkṣmaśarīre 'bhāvātkathaṃ sthūlaśarīrāśrayaṇamiti cet na dharmādyanvitabuddhyā saṃyogena tasyāpi dharmādyabhivāsitatvāt yathāhi surabhipuṣpādisambandhādvastramapi tadāmodavāsitaṃ bhavati / dharmādharmādinimittakaṃ ca sthūlaśarīragrahaṇaṃ tayoḥ saṃsargeṇa sūkṣmaśarīraṃ sthūlaśarīramāśritya devo vā manuṣyo vā paśurvā bhavati / yathāhi naṭastāṃ bhūmikāma vidhāya dharmarājo vā bhavati vatsarājo vā bhavati iti / hetustvatra puruṣārtha eva / tatrordhvagamanasya nimittaṃ dharmaḥ / evamadharmeṇādhogatiḥ / jñānena mokṣo 'jñānena bandhaḥ / tattvānabhijñasya puruṣasya vairāgyamātrātprakṛtyādiṣvātmabudhyopāsyamāneṣu tatraiva layaḥ rāgātsaṃsāraḥ aiśvaryādicchāyā avighātaḥ vighātaścānaiśvaryāt / ayaṃ buddhisargaḥ caturdhā viparyayāśaktituṣṭisiddhibhedāt / tatra viparyayo 'jñānamavidyā / viparyayaḥ pañcadhā avidyāsmitārāgadveṣābhiniveśā yathāsaṃkhyaṃ tamomohamahāmohatāmisrāndhatāmisrasaṃjñābhedāt / prakṛtyādiṣvanātmasvātmabuddhiravidyā tamaḥ / devādīnāmaṇidādyaiśvaryeṣu śāśvatikatvābhimāno 'smitā mohaḥ / śabdādiṣu viṣayeṣu rāga āsaktirmahāmohaḥ / devādīnāmasurādibhyaḥ svaiśvaryāṇimābhighātabhayamabhiniveśo 'ndhatāmisraḥ / aśaktistu andhatvapaṅgutvādirūpā karaṇavaikalyahetukā / tuṣṭayo dvedhā ādhyātmikā bāhyāśca prakṛtivyatirikta ātmāstīti niścitya saṃnyāsādeva tavāpavarto bhaviṣyatīti upadeśādau yā tuṣṭayastā ādhyātmikyaḥ pañcaviṣayoparamāt yā tuṣṭayastā bāhyāḥ / ātmavidyānāmadhyayanamananādayaḥ siddhibhedāḥ / evaṃ nirūpito buddhisargaḥ / tanmātrasargo 'pi devamanuṣyapaśvādibhedādbahudhā / tatrordhādhomadhyalokāḥ sattvarajotamobahulāḥ / nanu sukhaduḥkhādayaḥ prākṛtā buddhiguṇāḥ kathaṃ cetane bhavantīti cetsatyam puri liṅge śerate sa puruṣaḥ / evaṃ ca liṅgapuruṣayoḥ sambandhālliṅgadharmānātmanyadhyavasyati / ayaṃ ca mahadādi

  phalābhāve 'pi nirguṇe upakāriṇyapi puruṣe prakṛtistapasvinī pravartate eva yathāhi guṇavānupakāryapi bhṛtyo nirguṇe upakāriṇyapi svāmini niṣphalārādhanaḥ / yadyapi nāṭyānnivṛtto 'pi naṭaḥ kālāntare punarapi pravartate evaṃ muktaṃ prati prakṛtistu na punaḥ pravartate yathāhi vigalitavasanā kulavadhūḥ kadācitkenaciddṛṣṭā cettadāsau tathā yatate yathā na puruṣāntarāṇi paśyanti evaṃ prakṛtirapi vivekena sākṣātkṛtā 'tilajjāvaśātpunaḥ svātmānaṃ na pradarśayati / nanu savāsanakleśakarmāśayānāṃ bandhanasaṃjñitānāmapyapariṇāmini puruṣe 'sambhavātkathaṃ mokṣaḥ mucerbandhanaviśleṣārthatvāt / ata eva na saṃsāro 'pi sambhavati niṣkriyatvāt / maivam / yathāhi bhṛtyagatau jayaparājayau svāminyupacaryete evaṃ prakṛtigatayorapi bhogāpavargayorvivekāgrahātpuruṣe upacāraḥ / tatra dharmādharmājñānavairāgyāvairāgyaiśvaryānaiśvaryarūpaiḥ saptabhirbhāvairbadhnāti tattvajñānena tu mocayati / evaṃ ca kṛtādasmāttattvābhyāsānnāsmi na me nāhamiti śuddhamutpadyate jñānaṃ yadviṣayo abhyāsastaṃ sākṣātkārayatīti / nāsmītyanena kriyāmātranniṣidhyate asteḥ kriyārthatvāt / nāhamityanena kartṛtvaṃ na me ityanena svāmitvaṃ niṣidhyate / bhogavivekasākṣātkārau prakṛteḥ prasotavyau tau ca prasūtāviti nivṛttā prakṛtistāṃ niṣkriyaḥ svacchapuruṣaḥ paśyati prakṛtipuruṣayorasaṃsarge 'pyavivekakhyātinibandhanaḥ saṃsāraḥ punarna bhavati iti / ante tattvajñānasya tadānīmeva śarīrapātastu na bhavati / yathāhi nivṛtte kulālavyāpāre saṃskāravaśāt cakraṃ bhramattiṣṭhati evaṃ saṃskāravaśāt śarīramapi śarīrapātānantaraṃ tu pradhānasya nivṛttatvādātyantikamapi duḥkhaṃ naśyati duḥkhābhāvarūpaṃ kaivalyamāpnoti //
body.translated_text: Now the <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), which is useful for the knowledge of discrimination (<s>vivekajñāna</s>), is examined. Its function is <s>adhyavasāya</s> (determination/ascertainment), which is non-distinct from it. This is the defining characteristic of <s>buddhi</s>, because it distinguishes what is of the same and different class. For indeed, every transactor, having affirmed 'I am the authorized agent here,' determines 'this is to be done by me' and then proceeds. There, the determination 'this is to be done' — which belongs to <s>buddhi</s> that has acquired consciousness by virtue of the proximity of pure awareness (<s>citi</s>) — is the <s>adhyavasāya</s>. Among the functions [of <s>buddhi</s>]: <s>dharma</s> (virtue) is produced from the performance of sacrifice and the like; <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge) is the cognition of the otherness of <s>guṇa</s> and <s>puruṣa</s>; <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion) is the absence of passion. Similarly, <s>aiśvarya</s> (lordship) is also a function of <s>buddhi</s>, because the manifestation of [powers like] <s>aṇimā</s> (becoming minute) etc. proceeds from it. The <s>ahaṃkāra</s> (ego-sense) — the self-conceit of the kind 'I am capable here,' 'no one other than I is authorized here,' 'therefore I am' — is called <s>ahaṃkāra</s> because it is the function of the ego-sense. <s>Buddhi</s> indeed, relying on that [<s>ahaṃkāra</s>], determines 'this is to be done by me.' And from <s>ahaṃkāra</s> there is a twofold creation: the eleven sense organs from the <s>sāttvika</s> [<s>ahaṃkāra</s>], and the five <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements) from the <s>tāmasa</s>; as for <s>rajas</s>, its causality consists only in activating both. The names of <s>sāttvika</s>, <s>rājasa</s>, and <s>tāmasa</s> <s>ahaṃkāra</s> in order are: <s>vaikārika</s>, <s>taijasa</s>, and <s>bhūtādi</s>. The five cognitive sense organs (<s>buddhīndriya</s>) are called eye (<s>cakṣus</s>), ear (<s>śrotra</s>), nose (<s>ghrāṇa</s>), tongue (<s>rasana</s>), and skin (<s>tvac</s>). The five active sense organs (<s>karmendriya</s>) are speech (<s>vāk</s>), hands (<s>pāṇi</s>), feet (<s>pāda</s>), anus (<s>pāyu</s>), and genitals (<s>upastha</s>). The mind (<s>manas</s>) is of both kinds — both a cognitive organ and an active organ — because of the activity of the eye and other organs, when directed by the mind, in their respective objects. First, the cognition of an object — undifferentiated (<s>nirvikalpa</s>) like [the perception of] a young child or a mute — arises as knowledge in general; and then the determination by the properties of the object, such as class and so forth, is the function of the mind called <s>saṃkalpa</s> (constructive judgment). That the eleven types of sense organs arise from a single <s>ahaṃkāra</s> — here, the governing principle is only the distinction of <s>unseen merit</s> (<s>adṛṣṭabheda</s>) which sets in motion the enjoyment of sound and the like; and this distinction of <s>adṛṣṭa</s> is nothing but the transformation of the <s>guṇas</s>. The function of the five cognitive sense organs is the seeing of objects in contact [with them]; the functions of the active organs like speech are speaking and the rest. Thus, the function of <s>mahat</s> is <s>adhyavasāya</s> (determination); the function of <s>ahaṃkāra</s> is <s>abhimāna</s> (self-conceit); the function of <s>manas</s> is <s>saṃkalpa</s> (constructive judgment). There is no mixture of functions among the instruments directed toward their respective actions and effects — just as the <s>śāktīkas</s> and <s>yāṣṭīkas</s> (soldiers armed with spears and staffs), when they have set out to assail an enemy, take only their own spear and staff etc. and not the staff etc. of the other. [Objection:] Very well, since the <s>yāṣṭīkas</s> are conscious, they can proceed in that way; but since the instruments are insentient, their proceeding is unreasonable — therefore an overseer (<s>adhiṣṭhātā</s>) must be accepted, one who is conscious, familiar with the nature, power, and enjoyment of those instruments. [Reply:] Not so, because <s>puruṣa</s>'s [causal] function is that of the purpose (<s>puruṣārtha</s>) of that activity — this will be explained. The instruments are thirteen [in number]. Instrumentality (<s>karaṇatva</s>) for the cognitive organs means illuminating sound, touch, and the rest; for the active organs it means operating through speaking and similar activities. This external instrument [i.e., the five outer senses] operates in the present time; the inner instrument (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>), however, [operates] in all three times — [as evidenced by] the cognitions: 'From the flooding of the river, rain must have fallen,' 'There is fire, from smoke and so forth,' 'From the movement of ants [carrying eggs], there will be rain.' As for the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> who accept time as a single separate entity — even in their view, the distinction of conventional usage [of words like] 'past,' 'future,' etc. arises only from the distinction of [temporal] conditions (<s>upādhi</s>); and since these distinctions of past, future, etc. are established by precisely those conditions — what is the point of accepting a separate time-entity? So [argue] the Sāṃkhyas. And among these instruments there is also a ranking of primary and secondary. Just as village headmen collect taxes from cultivators and the like and hand them to the regional overseer, who [hands them] to the overseer of all, and he [hands them] to the king — in the same way, the outer sense organs, having observed [their objects], hand them over to <s>manas</s>; and <s>manas</s>, having constructed [them], to <s>ahaṃkāra</s>; and <s>ahaṃkāra</s>, having appropriated [them], to <s>buddhi</s>, which is the overseer of all. And these — <s>buddhi</s>, the sense organs, <s>manas</s>, and <s>ahaṃkāra</s> — are specific <s>guṇas</s>, modifications of the <s>guṇas</s> <s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s>; though mutually opposed, they have come to speak with one voice through the purpose of <s>puruṣa</s> — just as a lamp, which is composed of wick, oil, and flame, becomes illuminated when joined together by the removal of darkness. [Objection:] Why do [all the instruments] hand [their objects] to <s>buddhi</s> and not again to <s>ahaṃkāra</s> or to <s>manas</s>? [Reply:] Not so; because the primary direct instrument for the purpose of <s>puruṣa</s> is <s>buddhi</s> itself; <s>ahaṃkāra</s> and the rest are secondary in relation to it. The <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements) — such as sound, touch, and so forth — are undifferentiated (<s>aviśeṣa</s>) and subtle, not experienced [by us] as individually distinct. But in the gross [elements] such as ether: some are peaceful (<s>śānta</s>), pleasant, serene, light — because <s>sattva</s> predominates; some are fierce (<s>ghora</s>) and dull — because <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s> predominate. These [forms of the gross elements] are the specifics (<s>viśeṣas</s>). [The types of body are] again threefold: the subtle body (<s>sūkṣmaśarīra</s>), the body born of father and mother, and the gross elements (<s>mahābhūtas</s>). One subtle body was produced for each <s>puruṣa</s> by <s>pradhāna</s> at the beginning of creation; it penetrates even stone unobstructed. It persists from [the beginning of] creation until the great dissolution (<s>mahāpralaya</s>). This subtle body is the aggregate of <s>mahat</s>, <s>ahaṃkāra</s>, the eleven organs, and the five <s>tanmātras</s>. And because this body is not capable of experience, it resides in a gross body composed of the six sheaths (<s>ṣāṭkauśika</s>). The six sheaths are: hair, blood, flesh [from the mother]; sinews, bone, marrow [from the father]. [Objection:] Transmigration (<s>saṃsāra</s>) is caused by virtue and vice; since these are absent in the subtle body, how does it assume a gross body? [Reply:] Not so — because the subtle body is also pervaded by virtue and the rest through its conjunction with the <s>buddhi</s> that is endowed with virtue and the rest, just as a cloth pervaded with the fragrance of fragrant flowers etc. also becomes scented with that fragrance. And the assumption of a gross body is caused by virtue and vice; through the conjunction of these two, the subtle body, relying on a gross body, becomes a god, a human, or an animal. Just as an actor, by assuming a given role, becomes either a king of <s>dharma</s> (<s>dharmarāja</s>) or a cattle-king (<s>vatsarāja</s>). The cause in this is precisely the purpose of <s>puruṣa</s>. There, <s>dharma</s> (virtue) is the cause of upward movement; similarly, <s>adharma</s> (vice) [is the cause] of downward movement; liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>) [comes] through knowledge; bondage (<s>bandha</s>) through ignorance. For a <s>puruṣa</s> ignorant of the [twenty-five] <s>tattvas</s>: mere dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>) [from] <s>prakṛti</s> and the rest, when these are wrongly worshiped as the self, leads to dissolution (<s>laya</s>) in them; from passion, transmigration; from the desire for lordship etc., absence of obstruction; from want of lordship, obstruction. This <s>buddhi-creation</s> is fourfold, distinguished as <s>viparyaya</s> (error), <s>aśakti</s> (incapacity), <s>tuṣṭi</s> (contentment), and <s>siddhi</s> (attainment). Among these, <s>viparyaya</s> is ignorance (<s>ajñāna</s>), <s>avidyā</s>. <s>Viparyaya</s> is fivefold: <s>avidyā</s> (nescience), <s>asmitā</s> (ego), <s>rāga</s> (attachment), <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion), <s>abhiniveśa</s> (clinging to life) — respectively called by the names <s>tamas</s> (darkness), <s>moha</s> (delusion), <s>mahāmoha</s> (great delusion), <s>tāmisra</s> (gloom), and <s>andhatāmisra</s> (blind darkness). Treating <s>prakṛti</s> etc. — which are not self — as self is <s>avidyā</s>, [called] <s>tamas</s>. The conceit of permanence in the lordships such as the <s>aṇimā</s>-powers of gods etc. is <s>asmitā</s>, [called] <s>moha</s>. Attachment to sense objects like sound etc. is <s>rāga</s>, [called] <s>mahāmoha</s>. The fear of the destruction of one's lordship by the attack of demons etc. upon gods etc. is <s>abhiniveśa</s>, [called] <s>andhatāmisra</s>. <s>Aśakti</s> (incapacity) takes the form of blindness, lameness etc. and is caused by the deficiency of the [sense] instruments. The <s>tuṣṭis</s> (contentments) are of two kinds: inner (<s>ādhyātmika</s>) and external (<s>bāhya</s>). The inner [contentments] are [those] arising from instructions like: 'Having determined that there is a self distinct from <s>prakṛti</s>, renunciation alone will bring about your liberation.' The external [contentments] are those arising from the cessation of the five sense objects. The distinctions of <s>siddhi</s> (attainment) are: study of the knowledge of the self, reflection (<s>manana</s>), and so on. Thus the <s>buddhi-creation</s> has been examined. The <s>tanmātra-creation</s> too is manifold, due to the distinction into gods, humans, animals, and the like. Among these, the upper, lower, and middle worlds are respectively predominated by <s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s>. [Objection:] How do pleasure, pain, and the rest — which are [merely] the qualities of <s>buddhi</s> belonging to <s>prakṛti</s> — occur in the conscious [<s>puruṣa</s>]? [Reply:] True — '<s>puruṣa</s> lies in the abode of the liṅga [i.e., the subtle body].' And because of the connection of the <s>liṅga</s> (subtle body) and the <s>puruṣa</s>, the properties of the <s>liṅga</s> are ascribed to the self [by the uneducated]. This creation — from <s>mahat</s> to the gross elements including earth — is performed by <s>prakṛti</s> alone. If [the world were produced] without a cause, it would either always be [the case] or never be the case [that it is produced]. And the <s>Īśvara</s> (God) is not the material cause of it, because pure awareness (<s>citiśakti</s>) does not undergo transformation. Nor is it the case that <s>prakṛti</s> overseen by <s>Īśvara</s> is the agent, since an overseer who is without activity (<s>nirvyāpāra</s>) cannot [truly] oversee — for a carpenter who is without activity does not direct the axe, saw, and so on. [Objection:] If <s>prakṛti</s> is the agent, then, because of its permanence, it would never cease [creating], and liberation would never occur. [Reply:] Not so. Just as one who desires cooked rice does not start [cooking] again once the rice has been cooked, in the same way, <s>prakṛti</s> does not again proceed toward a <s>puruṣa</s> whom it has liberated. [Objection:] How can there be proceeding (<s>pravṛtti</s>), which is a property of the conscious, in <s>prakṛti</s> which is insentient? Therefore there must exist an overseer of <s>prakṛti</s> who is conscious; and since the [individual] <s>ātmans</s> do not know the nature of <s>prakṛti</s>, they are not fit to oversee it; therefore there exists an all-seeing overseer of <s>prakṛti</s> — and that is precisely <s>Īśvara</s>. [Reply:] True — just as milk, though insentient, flows for the growth of the calf, so <s>prakṛti</s> also will proceed for the liberation of <s>puruṣa</s>. And the proceeding of milk is not due to being overseen by <s>Īśvara</s>. For proceeding is of two kinds: for one's own purpose, or out of compassion. And <s>Īśvara</s>, whose every desire is fulfilled, has nothing to be desired; and before [the start of] creation there is no suffering, hence compassion would be impossible. Moreover, an <s>Īśvara</s> impelled by compassion would create only [beings who are] happy — not the variety [we see]. But since <s>prakṛti</s> is insentient, neither of these two [motivations apply]; rather, its proceeding is for another's purpose alone — just as an actor withdraws after having shown the spectators [the performance], so <s>prakṛti</s>, having revealed itself to the <s>puruṣa</s> in the form of sound etc. and as distinct from him, withdraws. Even though the <s>puruṣa</s> is without qualities and benefits [only through the action of <s>prakṛti</s>], <s>prakṛti</s> the austere one proceeds anyway — just as a servant, though capable and useful to a master who is capable, proceeds [uselessly] in fruitless service to a master without qualities. Although an actor who has withdrawn from the performance will again act at another time, <s>prakṛti</s> does not again proceed toward one who has been liberated — just as a woman of noble family, if once seen by someone in a state with her garment fallen [exposing herself], strives in such a way that other men do not see her; similarly, <s>prakṛti</s>, having been directly perceived with discrimination, out of extreme shame does not again reveal itself. [Objection:] Since the bonds — consisting of <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions), <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), <s>karman</s> (action-residues), and <s>āśaya</s> (mental deposits) — cannot occur in the unchanging <s>puruṣa</s>, how is liberation [possible]? Since liberation means the separation from bonds — and since transmigration also cannot occur because <s>puruṣa</s> is inactive. [Reply:] Not so. Just as victory and defeat belonging to the servant are figuratively attributed to the master, so too the enjoyment (<s>bhoga</s>) and liberation (<s>apavarga</s>) belonging to <s>prakṛti</s> are figuratively attributed to <s>puruṣa</s> through the failure to discriminate. There, through the seven dispositions (<s>bhāva</s>) — virtue, vice, ignorance, non-dispassion, dispassion, lordship, and its absence — [<s>prakṛti</s>] binds; but through knowledge of the <s>tattvas</s> it liberates. And thus, from the practice of these <s>tattvas</s>, pure knowledge arises: 'I am not [the body], nothing is mine, I am not [an ego]' — and the practice that has this [knowledge] as its object directly realizes it. By 'I am not,' the mere activity of being (<s>as</s>) is negated, since <s>as</s> is of the nature of activity. By 'I [am not],' agency is negated; by 'nothing is mine,' ownership is negated. The direct realization of discrimination and enjoyment must be produced by <s>prakṛti</s>; and when these have been produced, <s>prakṛti</s> has ceased; [and then] the inactive, pure <s>puruṣa</s> witnesses it. In the non-conjunction of <s>prakṛti</s> and <s>puruṣa</s>, transmigration does not occur again — which is bound only to the false cognition of non-discrimination. Ultimately, even at the time of the arising of that knowledge of <s>tattvas</s>, the body does not fall immediately. Just as, when the potter's activity has ceased, the wheel continues to spin by force of momentum — so by force of momentum, the body [continues] too. After the fall of the body, however, because <s>pradhāna</s> has ceased, even the ultimate suffering perishes; one attains <s>kaivalya</s> (absolute aloneness/liberation) — which is characterized by the absence of suffering.

Thus the <s>Tattvamīmāṃsā</s> (Inquiry into the Nature of Reality), composed by <s>Ācārya Kṛṣṇamitra</s>, son of the servant of <s>Gamasevaka</s>, son of the illustrious <s>Devīdatta</s>, is completed.
